The Qur'an: Textual Transmission and Historical Evidence

The same yardstick from Methodology is now applied to the Qur'an. The traditional account and the manuscript evidence are presented separately, then compared.

Part A — The traditional account

  • The Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad over c. 610–632 CE and memorized and written on scattered materials.
  • Under the caliph Abu Bakr a collection was made (motivated, the reports say, by the death of memorizers at the Battle of Yamama).
  • Under the caliph ʿUthman (c. 650 CE) a standardized consonantal rasm was promulgated and divergent codices were ordered destroyed (e.g., the codices associated with Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb).
  • The text was revealed, tradition holds, in *seven ahruf (modes); the canonical qiraʾat*** (readings) are the surviving regulated recitation traditions.

This account is internally coherent but is itself a tradition about history (Methodology §1.3) — its reliability is tested against physical evidence, not assumed.

Part B — The manuscript evidence

  • Birmingham folios (Mingana 1572a): parchment radiocarbon-dated to a very early range (with high probability before c. 645–660 CE). Its text is essentially the standard ʿUthmanic text — strong evidence that the standard consonantal skeleton was fixed very early.
  • Sanaa palimpsest (DAM 01-27.1): the most important find. The upper text is standard ʿUthmanic. The *erased lower text is a genuinely different, non-ʿUthmanic recension — a "companion codex" type. Studied by Behnam Sadeghi, Mohsen Goudarzi, and Asma Hilali, it shows real textual variants*: different words, word order, pronouns, and occasionally different formulae — precisely the kind of pre-standardization plurality the tradition itself describes (the burned codices).
  • Topkapi, Samarkand, Tübingen, Codex Parisino-petropolitanus and other early hijazi manuscripts: broadly confirm an early, stable consonantal rasm with orthographic development (dotting/vowelling added over time).

The reading traditions (qiraʾat)

  • The undotted early rasm could be vocalized differently. Ten qiraʾat became canonical. Today the world overwhelmingly uses Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿAṣim; Warsh ʿan Nafiʿ is used across much of North/West Africa.
  • Differences between, e.g., Ḥafṣ and Warsh are mostly vowels, pronunciation, and minor wording; a smaller number touch sense. Apologetically these are usually presented as a controlled, transmitted phenomenon — analogous in scale, defenders argue, to minor NT variants, not to wholesale change.

Academic positions

  • Mainstream (F. Déroche, B. Sadeghi, N. Sinai, A. Neuwirth, M. Cook): the ʿUthmanic consonantal text was standardized remarkably early (within ~2 decades of Muhammad's death); the Qur'an is best read as a genuine late-antique text of the early-mid 7th c. The Sanaa lower text proves early variation existed but was suppressed by standardization.
  • Revisionists (J. Wansbrough, P. Crone, M. Cook's early work): argued for much later canonization (8th–9th c.). The early manuscript datings (Birmingham, Sanaa) have substantially undercut the strong revisionist position, which is now a minority view.
  • Keith Small (Textual Criticism and Qurʾan Manuscripts): the ʿUthmanic standardization achieved textual unity by elimination of variants (destroying codices), whereas NT unity is reconstructed by comparison of surviving variants — two different models of "preservation."

Arbiter verdict — Qur'an transmission

Present.

  • Defense: an exceptionally early-fixed consonantal rasm (Birmingham), a strong oral-memorization tradition, and a globally near-uniform text today.
  • Prosecution: the standard text was achieved by destroying rival codices (so dissenting evidence was deliberately removed); the Sanaa lower text physically proves a different early recension existed; and the qiraʾat show the tradition is not, in fact, a single monolithic reading.

Weigh.

  • "The Qur'an's consonantal skeleton was standardized very early" — well supported by manuscripts; this is the Qur'an's genuine evidentiary strength.
  • "Therefore the Qur'an has been perfectly preserved with no variants" — not supported: Sanaa and the qiraʾat refute the strong form of that claim.
  • The ʿUthmanic model trades early uniformity for loss of the comparative evidence base — we cannot fully reconstruct the pre-ʿUthmanic plurality precisely because it was destroyed.

Judge. On the narrow historical question — was the standard text fixed early? — the evidence favors the Qur'an's defenders: standardization was impressively rapid and the resulting consonantal text is stable across the early manuscripts. On the absolute claim — the Qur'an has reached us with literally zero textual variation — the evidence favors the critics: the Sanaa palimpsest and the canonical qiraʾat are physical, internal counter-evidence. The defensible position is therefore: early and stable, but not variant-free, and "preserved by elimination" is a different historical claim from "preserved by abundant attestation."
